text.title: Requirement Quality Scorecard Core Rules
text.summary: 9 testable rules with rationale + source for requirement-quality-scorecard. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Each requirement MUST be scored on 6 axes: atomicity, testability, traceability, value, ambiguity (inverse), completeness — each 0/1/2.
rule.rationale: Quality delivered as a single verdict is unactionable: the author is told the requirement is weak and has to guess which property is missing, so revisions circle instead of converging. Decomposing into named attributes turns a verdict into a specific defect with a specific repair. The three-point band matters too, because a pass/fail scale pressures reviewers into passing anything borderline rather than blocking work, and the middle value is where most real requirements sit.

rule.statement: Atomicity=2 if requirement covers one verifiable behaviour; 1 if it covers a tightly grouped pair; 0 if it carries multiple behaviours that must be split.
rule.rationale: A requirement carrying several behaviours has no single verdict: it can be half-implemented and half-verified, so status, traceability and test coverage all report on something that is not one thing. It also hides scope, since two behaviours estimated as one item get estimated at the size of the smaller. The middle band exists because forcing a split on a genuinely coupled pair yields two fragments neither of which is meaningful alone.

rule.statement: Testability=2 if a test case can be written without ambiguity; 1 if a test exists but needs interpretation; 0 if no test is derivable.
rule.rationale: The test case is the operational definition of the requirement, so where none can be derived the meaning has not actually been fixed and acceptance becomes a negotiation held at the point of maximum cost and minimum goodwill. Attempting the derivation during review is cheap and exposes the gap while the requirement is still soft. The middle band flags the requirement whose test exists only after the tester supplies an interpretation, which is precisely where divergence enters unnoticed.

rule.statement: Traceability=2 if forward + backward links exist (to need + to design / test); 1 if only one direction; 0 if absent.
rule.rationale: The two directions answer different questions and each absence has its own failure. With no backward link to a need, a requirement cannot be justified when scope is cut, so gold-plating survives the cut and something necessary goes instead. With no forward link to design and test, a need can pass through delivery with nothing built against it until the client exercises it. Scoring one direction as partial reflects that half a chain leaves one of those holes fully open.

rule.statement: Ambiguity is scored inverse: 2 = no ambiguous terms; 1 = 1-2 weak words (may, should); 0 = 3+ weak words or undefined glossary terms.
rule.rationale: Weak modals let every reader resolve the sentence toward their own expectation, and the damage is that the divergence is invisible: everyone leaves the review believing they agreed, and the disagreement appears only in the built system. Counting the weak words turns a soft property into something a reviewer, or a script, can check consistently rather than score by mood. Undefined glossary terms are the same defect at domain scale, since one contested term ambiguates every requirement that uses it.

rule.statement: Baseline requires aggregate score at least 10 / 12; below that, requirement returns to drafting with annotated weaknesses.
rule.rationale: A scorecard with no gate becomes a report that is filed and not acted on, because schedule pressure always produces an argument that this particular requirement is good enough to proceed. Attaching a number to the baseline moves that argument from the individual requirement to the threshold, where it is had once and in public. Returning the requirement with its weak axes annotated, rather than as a bare rejection, is what keeps the rework targeted instead of sending the author back to guessing.

rule.statement: Each axis score MUST cite evidence (test case id, glossary entry, parent epic); un-evidenced scores forbidden.
rule.rationale: An unevidenced score records a reviewer's impression, and impressions drift between reviewers and across weeks, so the same requirement scores differently depending on who opened it and when, destroying the comparability the scorecard exists to provide. The citation also does work beyond the audit trail: producing the test case id or glossary entry forces the reviewer to confirm it exists, which catches the common case where traceability was assumed rather than checked.

rule.statement: Reviewer named per axis when scores diverge; anonymous scoring forbidden.
rule.rationale: Divergent scores are the most valuable signal the scorecard produces, because they pinpoint the axis on which two competent readers understood the requirement differently, which is where the real ambiguity lives. Anonymity destroys that signal: the split is visible but neither reader can be asked what they saw, so the disagreement gets averaged away instead of resolved. Naming the reviewer on the divergent axis turns a number back into a conversation.

rule.statement: If the engagement has fewer than 20 requirements or no baseline event, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: The scorecard earns its overhead through comparability across a body of requirements; below roughly twenty a reviewer can hold the whole set in mind at once, and inconsistency between them is not yet the dominant defect. The absence of a baseline event is the more decisive condition: with no moment at which requirements are frozen there is nothing for the threshold to gate, and scores carrying no consequence are exactly the measurement theatre the threshold rule exists to prevent.
